entities.summary:
François de Mailly (1658–1721), a scion of a prominent Picard noble family, emerged as a significant ecclesiastical and political figure in late 17th and early 18th-century France. Born in Paris on March 4, 1658, he ascended through the ranks of the Catholic Church during a period marked by intense theological debates, particularly between Gallicanism and Ultramontanism, and the ongoing struggle against Jansenism. His career, culminating in his elevation to Cardinal, positioned him as a key advisor to the French monarchy and a prominent voice within the French episcopate, influencing both church governance and state-church relations under Louis XIV and the Regency.

After a distinguished education at the Sorbonne, de Mailly was appointed Archbishop of Arles in 1697, a position he held until 1710. His administrative acumen and loyalty to the crown were recognized, leading to his transfer to the prestigious Archbishopric of Reims in 1710, a see traditionally associated with the coronation of French monarchs. Throughout his tenure, de Mailly was a staunch defender of royal prerogatives over papal authority, aligning himself with the Gallican tenets that asserted the independence of the French Church from Rome in temporal matters. He actively participated in the condemnation of Jansenist doctrines, notably supporting the papal bull *Unigenitus* in 1713, which further cemented his standing within the conservative ecclesiastical establishment.
